questions.q: What does "capability" measure in a model, as distinct from alignment?
options: How closely the model's objective matches what its designers intended
How effectively the model achieves whatever objective it is actually pursuing
How large the model's parameter count is
How many safety evaluations the model has passed
questions.explain: Capability is about effectiveness at achieving some objective, whatever that objective happens to be. It says nothing about whether the objective itself is the right one.

questions.q: Why can a highly capable system still be badly misaligned?
options: Capability and alignment are the same property measured differently
Capable systems are always trained with more human feedback
Capability measures effectiveness at pursuing a goal, and that goal can still be the wrong one
Misalignment only happens in systems with low capability
questions.explain: A highly capable system is just very effective at pursuing whatever it's actually optimizing for. If that target diverges from what designers intended, high capability makes the divergence more consequential, not less.

questions.q: In this course's working definition, what does the word "reliably" emphasize about alignment?
options: That a model only needs to behave well on its training distribution
That alignment must hold across situations the system actually encounters, not only the ones it was trained or tested on
That alignment is a legal requirement set by regulators
That reliability is measured purely by uptime and latency
questions.explain: Behaving as intended during training or evaluation isn't sufficient — the definition requires the intended behavior to hold up under distribution shift and novel situations too.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes outer alignment from inner alignment, as previewed in this lesson?
options: Outer alignment is about model size; inner alignment is about training data size
Outer alignment asks if the specified/trained objective is the right one; inner alignment asks if the resulting model actually internalized that objective
Outer alignment applies only to language models; inner alignment applies only to robotics
They are two names for the exact same concept
questions.explain: Outer alignment concerns the target you aim training at. Inner alignment concerns whether the trained model actually ends up pursuing that target rather than some other goal that happened to score well.

questions.q: Why is alignment treated as a distinct problem from simply improving a model's capability?
options: Because more capable models are automatically better aligned
Because capability only applies to narrow AI, not general systems
Because increasing capability amplifies whatever objective a system is pursuing without correcting its direction
Because alignment and capability are measured on an identical scale
questions.explain: Capability makes a system more effective at whatever it's actually optimizing for. It does not, by itself, make that objective more likely to match the designers' intent — which is why alignment requires separate attention.
